title: Ferris v. Amazon.com Services, LLC — Order on AI-Fabricated Citations by a Pro Se Litigant (N.D. Miss.)
author: United States District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi (Mills · S.J.)

st.t: Filing duties: AI use never displaces inquiry
st.an: Ferris directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition by applying Rule 11’s reasonable-inquiry duty to false citations and treating continued use after notice as a violation. It also confirms that sanctions must be selected within a proportionate, discretionary framework; the excerpt indicates only an initial inclination toward dismissal, not a final sanction.

Ferris violated Rule 11 by submitting false citations to the Court—first, in his complaint; then, after being put on notice by Defendant, in his subsequent filings.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures

It also reinforces the cluster’s concern that fabricated citations shift disproportionate verification costs to courts and opposing parties, without establishing a general model error rate or a distinct AI-specific sanctions rule.

kp.k: AI-generated false citations persisted after explicit notice
kp.d: The court records that pro se plaintiff William Ferris cited a nonexistent case in his August 26, 2024 complaint, then submitted six cases the court characterized as fake after Amazon identified the original fabrication. Three further filings arriving on March 3, 2025 contained false or misleading citations. At the April 8, 2025 show-cause hearing, Ferris acknowledged using AI to draft the problematic filings; his hearing statement was also AI-drafted. This is evidence from an individual sanctions proceeding, not a measurement of model error rates.
qs: Amazon pointed out that Mr. Ferris' Eastman-Kodak citation was fictional.
That same day, three filings by Mr. Ferris arrived by mail—all containing false or misleading citations.

On April 8, 2025, a show-cause hearing was held during which Mr. Ferris informed the Court that he had drafted the problematic filings using AI. The statement Mr. Ferris read to the Court was also drafted by AI.

kp.k: Cheap generation shifts verification burdens onto courts and opponents
kp.d: The court argues that careless AI use produces plausible legal fiction much faster than others can check it. Opposing parties and courts must inspect case names, citations and legal propositions to separate truth from fabrication. Its broader claim that proliferation places significant strain on the judicial system is qualitative reasoning in the order, rather than a quantified workload finding.
qs: When used carelessly, it produces frustratingly realistic legal fiction that takes inordinately longer to respond to than to create.

While one party can create a fake legal brief at the click of a button, the opposing party and court must parse through the case names, citations, and points of law to determine which parts, if any, are true.
As AI continues to proliferate, this creation-response imbalance places significant strain on the judicial system.

kp.k: The court distinguishes prudent AI use from harmful misuse
kp.d: The order acknowledges potential benefits from prudent AI use while condemning persistent misrepresentation of law as undermining fair adjudication. Its criticism is directed at careless use and false authority, rather than treating AI use itself as the violation.
qs: Courts exist to decide controversies fairly, in accordance with the law. This function is undermined when litigants using AI persistently misrepresent the law to the courts.
AI is a powerful tool, that when used prudently, provides immense benefits.

kp.k: Rule 11 obligations extend to self-represented AI users
kp.d: The court applies Rule 11's reasonable-inquiry requirement to all parties, including pro se litigants, and finds Ferris violated it through false citations in his complaint and subsequent filings after notice. The order grounds accountability in existing litigation obligations, not a newly created AI-specific rule.
qs: Rule 11, which applies to all parties, including pro se litigants
Litigants "have a duty 'to conduct a reasonable inquiry into the facts or law before filing the lawsuit.'"
Mr. Ferris violated Rule 11 by submitting false citations to the Court—first, in his complaint; then, after being put on notice by Defendant, in his subsequent filings.

kp.k: Cost sanctions replace dismissal and target attributable expenses
kp.d: Although initially inclined to dismiss the case, the court interprets Fifth Circuit authorities as favoring less final sanctions and orders Ferris to pay Amazon's costs attributable to responding to fabricated citations. It identifies this as the least drastic adequate deterrent, subject to Amazon's duty to mitigate. The April 16, 2025 order sets no monetary amount: reasonable attributable costs and expenses must be documented before a subsequent determination.
qs: This Court is initially inclined to dismiss Mr. Ferris' case due to the numerous fake citations cited by him. However, an examination of relevant Fifth Circuit authorities indicates that the appellate courts are inclined toward less final sanctions in these regards.

Mr. Ferris must pay the costs incurred by Defendant attributable to responding to Mr. Ferris' fabricated citations, keeping in mind Defendant's duty to mitigate, this being the least drastic sanction to deter "comparable conduct by others similarly situated."
Defendant shall submit a detailed bill of costs, with accompanying affidavit, showing what costs and expenses were incurred as a reasonable result of Plaintiff's false citations.
Once the bill of costs and affidavit have been submitted, this Court will determine the exact amount Plaintiff owes in a subsequent order.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Judge Michael P. Mills argues that careless AI use generates convincing false legal material cheaply, shifting disproportionately time-consuming verification work to opponents and courts and straining the judicial system.
pts.d: The order contrasts unspecified benefits of prudent AI use with the concrete harms of careless use: realistic fabricated authority, an imbalance between the effort required to create and respond to a filing, and interference with fair adjudication. Mills anticipates continuing systemic strain as AI proliferates. The order also establishes a concrete consequence in this case: a self-represented litigant's submission of fabricated citations, including after notice, violated Rule 11 and required payment of the defendant's attributable response costs. It does not treat AI use itself as the violation or announce a prohibition on AI-assisted filings.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on the court's experience with repeated fabricated citations in this litigation and the litigant's acknowledgment of AI use; the sanction rests on Rule 11 and Fifth Circuit authority.
pts.d: The order identifies one nonexistent authority in the complaint, six fake cases in the response to the motion to dismiss, and three further filings containing false or misleading citations. Ferris told the court at the show-cause hearing that he used AI to draft the problematic filings. These case-specific observations support the discussion of verification burdens; no measured response times, aggregate caseload data, model benchmarks, or hallucination rates are supplied. The assertion of immense benefits is not supported with examples or data. Mills cites Rule 11 and Skidmore, Thomas, and Willy in explaining reasonable inquiry, sanctions, proportionality, and mitigation. The exact monetary burden remained to be determined.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The order describes an existing problem in 2024–2025 and projects continuing strain as AI adoption expands, without specifying a forecast horizon.
pts.d: The litigation began on August 26, 2024; the court found a Rule 11 violation on March 3, 2025, heard Ferris on April 8, and ordered costs on April 16. The harm claim is conditional on careless AI use and persistent misrepresentation, whereas the benefits claim is conditional on prudent use. The sanction reflects repeated false citations after notice, rather than a general prediction that all AI users will face sanctions. Mills considered dismissal but selected attributable costs as the least severe adequate sanction, subject to the defendant's duty to mitigate and later determination of the amount.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Opposing parties and courts bear verification burdens; litigants, including those without lawyers, retain responsibility for their filings and face financial consequences for false citations.
pts.d: Amazon incurred costs responding to Ferris's fabricated authorities, while the court had to address repeated misleading filings and conduct sanction proceedings. Ferris, a self-represented employee suing his employer, was ordered to pay reasonable attributable costs rather than have his case dismissed as a sanction in this order. More broadly, Mills identifies a threat to the judiciary's ability to decide controversies fairly and seeks deterrence of similarly situated litigants. The source does not make claims about law-firm staffing, legal-market pricing, or improved access to justice.
